stem: Which of these is NOT one of the four Coffman conditions that must all hold for a deadlock?

options.text: Hold and wait: a thread keeps one resource while it waits for another
options.why: This is one of the four conditions: holding while waiting is what lets waits chain together.

options.text: Unfair scheduling: the lock does not grant waiters in arrival order
options.why: Unfairness can cause starvation, but deadlock needs no particular scheduling policy.

options.text: No preemption: a resource cannot be forcibly taken from its holder
options.why: This is one of the four conditions: if resources could be taken away, the wait could be broken.

options.text: Circular wait: a closed chain of threads each waits for the next one
options.why: This is one of the four conditions and the one most designs break with lock ordering.

explanation: Coffman et al. (1971) listed four necessary conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. All four must hold at once for a deadlock. Fairness is about starvation, a different liveness failure in which a thread waits indefinitely while others keep making progress.
reference: Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani, System Deadlocks (1971)

stem: Because all four Coffman conditions must hold at the same time for a deadlock, a design that reliably prevents any one of them cannot deadlock on those resources.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: the conditions are jointly necessary, so removing one removes the possibility of deadlock.

options.text: False
options.why: They are necessary conditions, so eliminating any single one is enough to rule deadlock out.

explanation: This is why practical prevention techniques each target one condition: lock ordering breaks circular wait, acquiring everything up front breaks hold and wait, and try-lock with release simulates preemption. Note the claim is about deadlock only: a design can still livelock or starve.
reference: Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani, System Deadlocks (1971)

stem: Match each Coffman condition with a description of it.

options.text: Only one thread can use the resource at a time
A thread holds at least one resource while requesting another
A resource is released only voluntarily by its holder
Threads form a cycle, each waiting on the next

explanation: These are the four necessary conditions for deadlock. Each prevention strategy attacks one of them: sharable or lock-free resources attack mutual exclusion, all-at-once acquisition attacks hold and wait, try-lock with release or timeouts approximate preemption, and a global lock order removes circular wait.
reference: Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani, System Deadlocks (1971)

stem:
Two threads run `transfer(a, b, 10)` and `transfer(b, a, 20)` at the same time. What can go wrong?

```python
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    with src.lock:
        with dst.lock:
            src.balance -= amount
            dst.balance += amount
```

options.text: Nothing: each `with` block releases its lock before the next one starts
options.why: The inner `with` runs while the outer lock is still held, so each thread holds one lock while waiting.

options.text: Each thread can take its first lock and then wait forever for the other
options.why: Thread 1 holds a and waits for b while thread 2 holds b and waits for a: a circular wait.

options.text: The balances can go negative because the two updates interleave
options.why: Both updates run with both locks held, so they cannot interleave.

options.text: Python raises a RuntimeError because the same lock is used twice
options.why: Each thread uses two different locks once each; no error is raised.

explanation: The locks are taken in argument order, so the two calls take them in opposite orders. If thread 1 acquires `a.lock` and thread 2 acquires `b.lock` before either takes its second lock, each waits forever for the other. The standard fix is to acquire locks in a consistent global order, for example by account id.

stem: Safety properties say "something bad never happens"; liveness properties say "something good eventually happens". Which of these is a liveness property?

options.text: At most one thread is inside the critical section at any moment
options.why: This forbids a bad state (two threads inside), so it is a safety property.

options.text: Every thread that requests the lock eventually acquires it
options.why: This promises eventual progress, which is the definition of a liveness property.

options.text: An account balance is never observed in a half-updated state
options.why: This forbids a bad observation, so it is a safety property.

options.text: A released lock is never held by two threads at the same time
options.why: This also forbids a bad state, so it is a safety property.

explanation: Deadlock freedom, starvation freedom and lock-out freedom are liveness properties: they require that something eventually happens. Mutual exclusion and invariant preservation are safety properties. A system can be perfectly safe (never corrupts data) and still have no liveness (it deadlocks), which is why both must be argued separately.
reference: Lamport, Proving the Correctness of Multiprocess Programs (1977)

stem:
The `transfer` function is changed to always lock the account with the smaller `id` first, then the other one. Which Coffman condition does this fix break?

```python
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    with src.lock:
        with dst.lock:
            src.balance -= amount
            dst.balance += amount
```

options.text: Mutual exclusion, because the ordered locks can now be shared
options.why: Each lock is still exclusive; only the order in which they are taken changed.

options.text: Hold and wait, because a thread never holds a lock while it waits
options.why: A thread still holds the first lock while waiting for the second one.

options.text: No preemption, because a waiting thread can now take the lock away
options.why: Nothing forcibly takes a lock away; waiting threads still just wait.

options.text: Circular wait, as every thread takes both locks in one fixed order
options.why: With a single global order, a cycle of waiters cannot form.

explanation: If every thread acquires locks in increasing id order, a thread holding lock i can only wait for a lock j > i. A cycle would need some thread to wait for a smaller id than one it holds, which the ordering forbids. Mutual exclusion, hold and wait and no preemption all still apply, but circular wait cannot, so deadlock is impossible.

stem: A job runner changes its design so that each job requests every lock it will need in a single atomic step before doing any work, and takes none if any is unavailable. Which Coffman condition does this break?

options.text: Hold and wait, as a job never holds locks while it waits for others
options.why: All-or-nothing acquisition means a waiting job holds nothing.

options.text: Circular wait, since the locks are now always acquired in sorted order
options.why: The design says nothing about order; it avoids holding while waiting.

options.text: No preemption, since the runner can take locks away from slow jobs
options.why: Nothing is taken away from a holder; jobs simply never wait while holding.

options.text: Mutual exclusion, since a lock can now be held by several jobs at once
options.why: Each lock is still exclusive to one job at a time.

explanation: Requesting all resources at once (or releasing everything when any request fails) means a job is either running with everything it needs or holding nothing. That removes hold and wait. The costs are lower concurrency, since locks are held longer than needed, and the need to know every resource up front, which is often impractical.
reference: Silberschatz et al., Operating System Concepts, §8.5

options.text: It prints 42, because `inner` runs on a spare thread the pool creates
options.why: The pool never grows beyond `max_workers`, so no spare thread exists.

options.text: It raises RuntimeError because a task may not submit to its own pool
options.why: Submitting from a worker is allowed; the problem is blocking on the result.

options.text: It hangs: `outer` occupies the only worker while waiting for `inner`
options.why: `inner` is queued behind `outer`, which never finishes because it waits for `inner`.

options.text: It prints 42 because `result()` runs the queued task inline
options.why: `Future.result()` only waits; it never executes the task itself.

explanation: This is thread-pool starvation deadlock. The single worker runs `outer`, which submits `inner` and blocks on its result. `inner` sits in the queue waiting for a free worker, but the only worker is the one blocked. Verified on Python 3.13: `result(timeout=1)` raises `TimeoutError`, and with `max_workers=2` the same code prints 42. Avoid blocking on futures from inside the same bounded pool.

stem:
What happens when this Go program runs?

```go
func main() {
    ch := make(chan int)
    ch <- 1
    fmt.Println(<-ch)
}
```

options.text: It prints 1, because the send is buffered until the receive below it
options.why: An unbuffered channel has no buffer: a send blocks until another goroutine receives.

options.text: It crashes with "fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!"
options.why: main blocks on the send and no other goroutine exists to receive, so the runtime aborts.

options.text: It blocks forever silently, because Go cannot detect blocked sends
options.why: The runtime does detect the case where every goroutine is blocked.

options.text: It panics with "send on closed channel" because nothing reads it
options.why: The channel is never closed; that panic only happens after close().

explanation: An unbuffered channel send completes only when a receiver takes the value. The only goroutine is main, and it is stuck on the send, so the receive on the next line is never reached. When every goroutine is blocked, the Go runtime reports "fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!". Fixes: make the channel buffered (`make(chan int, 1)`) or receive in another goroutine.
reference: The Go Programming Language Specification: Send statements

stem:
Which two changes would prevent the deadlock between concurrent `transfer(a, b, …)` and `transfer(b, a, …)` calls? (Choose two.)

```python
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    with src.lock:
        with dst.lock:
            src.balance -= amount
            dst.balance += amount
```

options.text: Acquire the two locks in a fixed order, such as by account id
options.why: A global order makes a cycle of waiters impossible.

options.text: Guard every transfer with one global lock instead of per-account locks
options.why: With a single lock there is nothing to wait for while holding another lock.

options.text: Replace each `Lock` with an `RLock` so the locks become reentrant
options.why: Reentrancy only helps the same thread re-acquire its own lock, not opposite orders.

options.text: Add `time.sleep(0.01)` between taking the first and second lock
options.why: Sleeping while holding the first lock makes the deadlock window larger.

options.text: Run more worker threads so that one of them can always make progress
options.why: The two stuck threads still wait on each other no matter how many others exist.

explanation: Deadlock needs a circular wait among threads holding locks. Ordering lock acquisition removes the cycle; a single coarse lock removes the possibility of holding one lock while waiting for another (at the cost of serialising all transfers). Reentrant locks, sleeps and extra threads leave the opposite-order acquisition untouched.

stem:
Two threads each run this loop with the same lock pair in opposite orders. Both threads are using CPU, yet neither ever finishes. What is happening, and what fixes it?

```python
while True:
    first.acquire()
    if second.acquire(blocking=False):
        break
    first.release()
    time.sleep(0.01)  # back off, then retry
```

options.text: Deadlock; use `RLock` so each thread can re-enter the lock it holds
options.why: The threads are not blocked; they keep acquiring and releasing, which is livelock.

options.text: Starvation of one thread; switch to a fair lock with FIFO hand-off
options.why: Both threads fail repeatedly in lockstep; fairness does not break the symmetry.

options.text: Priority inversion; raise the priority of the thread that waits longer
options.why: No priorities are involved; the threads are equal and keep colliding.

options.text: Livelock: both back off in lockstep; use randomised, growing back-off
options.why: Random jitter makes it unlikely the threads keep colliding on every retry.

explanation: Each thread repeatedly takes its first lock, fails to get the second, releases and retries after the same fixed delay. If they stay in step, they collide forever while burning CPU: livelock. A randomised (and usually exponentially growing) back-off breaks the symmetry. Alternatively, remove the opposite orders entirely with a global lock order.
reference: Herlihy and Shavit, The Art of Multiprocessor Programming, §7.4

stem: In Python, calling `threading.current_thread().join()` from inside a thread deadlocks that thread forever.

options.text: True
options.why: Python checks for this case and raises instead of blocking forever.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `join()` raises `RuntimeError: cannot join current thread` rather than deadlocking.

explanation: A thread waiting for itself to finish could never succeed, so CPython detects it up front: `Thread.join()` raises `RuntimeError("cannot join current thread")`. Verified on Python 3.13. The same check fires indirectly when a worker calls `ThreadPoolExecutor.shutdown(wait=True)` on its own executor, because shutdown joins every worker thread.

stem: Which two situations can cause starvation, where a thread waits indefinitely even though the system as a whole keeps making progress? (Choose two.)

options.text: A reader-preferring read-write lock under a steady stream of overlapping readers
options.why: New readers keep joining, so the read count never drops to zero and a writer never gets in.

options.text: Strict priority scheduling with a continuous supply of high-priority work
options.why: A low-priority thread is ready but never chosen while higher-priority work keeps arriving.

options.text: A FIFO ticket lock where each waiter takes a number and is served in order
options.why: Ticket locks are fair: every waiter is served after a bounded number of others.

options.text: Two threads that each hold one lock and wait forever for the other lock
options.why: That is deadlock: no thread makes progress, not just one.

options.text: A bounded queue whose producer blocks only while the queue is completely full
options.why: The producer resumes as soon as a consumer takes an item; it is not starved.

explanation: Starvation differs from deadlock: the system progresses, but a particular thread does not. Reader preference can starve writers; strict priorities can starve low-priority threads. The usual cures are fairness (FIFO hand-off, writer preference once a writer is waiting) and aging, which slowly raises the priority of threads that have waited a long time.
reference: Silberschatz et al., Operating System Concepts, §5.7 and §6.3

stem: A Python thread already holds `lock = threading.Lock()` and then calls `lock.acquire(timeout=0.2)` again. What does that call return? Type the value.
explanation: A `threading.Lock` is not reentrant: the second acquire waits for the lock to be released, which only the same thread could do. With a timeout the call gives up after 0.2 seconds and returns `False` (verified on Python 3.13); without a timeout the thread would deadlock with itself. An `RLock` would return `True` because it tracks its owner and a recursion count.

stem: Put the steps of how a database such as PostgreSQL resolves a deadlock between two transactions in order.

options.text: The aborted transaction gets a deadlock error and its locks are released
It finds a cycle in the wait-for graph and chooses one transaction to abort
Two transactions each hold a row lock the other one needs, and both start waiting
After a lock wait exceeds the deadlock timeout, the database checks the waits for a cycle
The surviving transaction acquires the lock and continues; the application retries the aborted one

explanation: Databases allow deadlocks to happen and then detect them. PostgreSQL waits `deadlock_timeout` (default 1 second) before running the comparatively expensive check, then searches the wait-for graph for a cycle. One transaction is aborted with error 40P01; which one is not predictable, so the application must be ready to retry it.

stem: A database lock manager has this wait-for graph, where `X → Y` means "X is waiting for a lock Y holds": `T1 → T2`, `T2 → T3`, `T3 → T1`, `T4 → T1`. Which transactions are deadlocked?

options.text: All four, because every transaction is currently blocked on another one
options.why: T4 is blocked but not part of a cycle; it can proceed once T1 finishes or is aborted.

options.text: T1, T2 and T3; T4 is only waiting behind the cycle
options.why: Only the transactions on the cycle can never progress without intervention.

options.text: Only T1, because it is the one that both T3 and T4 are waiting for
options.why: T1 is on the cycle, but so are T2 and T3, which wait on each other in turn.

options.text: None of them yet, because a deadlock requires a cycle of exactly two
options.why: A cycle of any length is a deadlock; three transactions can form one.

explanation: A deadlock corresponds to a cycle in the wait-for graph. T1 → T2 → T3 → T1 is a cycle, so those three are deadlocked. T4 waits for T1 but nothing waits for T4, so it is merely blocked: aborting any one of T1, T2 or T3 breaks the cycle, and T4 then proceeds when T1 releases its locks.
reference: Silberschatz et al., Operating System Concepts, §8.6

stem: Which three of these can deadlock even though the code never touches a mutex explicitly? (Choose three.)

options.text: A Go `main` that sends on an unbuffered channel no other goroutine reads
options.why: The send waits for a receiver that can never run.

options.text: Tasks in a fixed-size pool that each block on subtasks submitted to that pool
options.why: Once every worker is blocked waiting, the queued subtasks have no thread to run on.

options.text: A coroutine that calls `run_coroutine_threadsafe(coro, same_loop).result()`
options.why: It blocks the loop thread, which is the only thread that could run `coro`.

options.text: A Go goroutine that receives from a channel that has already been closed
options.why: Receiving from a closed channel returns the zero value immediately; it never blocks.

options.text: A Node.js async function that awaits a promise which is already resolved
options.why: Awaiting a resolved promise just resumes on the next microtask.

explanation: Deadlock only needs threads (or tasks) waiting on each other in a cycle; the resource can be a channel, a pool slot or the event-loop thread itself. Verified for C on Python 3.13: `fut.result(timeout=0.5)` raises TimeoutError because the loop is blocked by the very call waiting on it. Closed-channel receives and resolved promises never block.
reference: Python docs: asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe; Go spec: Receive operator

stem: A system has 12 units of one resource. P0 holds 5 and may need up to 10; P1 holds 2 and may need up to 4; P2 holds 2 and may need up to 9. Using the Banker's algorithm, type the safe sequence (for example `P2, P1, P0`).
explanation: Available = 12 − (5 + 2 + 2) = 3. Remaining needs: P0 5, P1 2, P2 7. Only P1 (need 2 ≤ 3) can finish first; it returns its 2, so 5 are available. Then P0 (need 5 ≤ 5) finishes and returns 5, leaving 10, enough for P2 (need 7). The state is safe with the unique sequence P1, P0, P2 (checked with a short simulation).
reference: Silberschatz et al., Operating System Concepts, §8.6.3

stem: A real-time system has three tasks. Low-priority L holds mutex M. High-priority H wakes up and blocks on M. Medium-priority Med, which never touches M, becomes ready and runs for a long time. What is happening, and what is the standard fix?

options.text: Deadlock between H and L; acquire M with a timeout in H
options.why: There is no cycle: L would release M if it could run.

options.text: Starvation of Med; give Med a time slice so it yields to L
options.why: Med is the one running; the problem is that it delays H indirectly.

options.text: Priority inversion; give L H's priority via inheritance
options.why: Boosting L lets it preempt Med, finish its critical section and release M.

options.text: A convoy; replace M with a spinlock so H acquires it faster
options.why: Spinning in H would only waste CPU while L still cannot run.

explanation: H effectively runs at L's priority because it is waiting on L, and Med preempts L, so a medium-priority task delays the highest-priority one for an unbounded time. With priority inheritance, L temporarily inherits H's priority while H waits on M, so Med can no longer preempt it. The priority ceiling protocol is the other common remedy.
reference: Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky, Priority Inheritance Protocols (1990)

stem: In 1997 NASA's Mars Pathfinder lander kept resetting itself after a watchdog timer expired. The cause was priority inversion on a mutex shared by a high-priority bus task and a low-priority meteorological task. How did engineers fix it?

options.text: They rewrote the bus task to stop using the shared mutex
options.why: The fix was a configuration change, not a rewrite of the task.

options.text: They uploaded a patch turning on priority inheritance for it
options.why: VxWorks supported priority inheritance; it had been turned off for that mutex.

options.text: They lengthened the watchdog timeout so the resets stopped
options.why: A longer timeout would only hide the stall, not remove the inversion.

options.text: They lowered the priority of the communications task
options.why: Medium-priority work preempting the lock holder was the problem, not the bus task.

explanation: The VxWorks mutex was created with priority inheritance disabled. Medium-priority communication tasks preempted the low-priority task holding the mutex, so the high-priority bus task missed its deadline and the watchdog reset the system. Engineers reproduced it on Earth and uploaded a patch that turned priority inheritance on for that mutex.
reference: Reeves, What Really Happened on Mars? (1997)

stem: Match each technique with how it limits priority inversion.

options.text: Raises the lock holder's priority only when a higher-priority task blocks on the lock
Raises a task to the highest priority of any user of the lock as soon as it locks it
Prevents all preemption while any critical section runs
Retries failed lock attempts after a random delay

explanation: Priority inheritance boosts the holder on demand. The immediate priority ceiling protocol boosts a task to the lock's ceiling as soon as it acquires it, which also prevents chained blocking and deadlock among locks managed this way. Disabling preemption is the bluntest tool: it bounds inversion but delays every other task. Random back-off is a livelock remedy and does not address priorities.
reference: Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky, Priority Inheritance Protocols (1990)

stem: Threads take lock A, then try lock B with a non-blocking try-lock and retry on failure. Which three statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: If every thread retries after the same fixed delay, they can livelock
options.why: Threads that fail in lockstep keep colliding on each retry.

options.text: Randomised exponential back-off makes repeated collisions unlikely
options.why: Jitter breaks the symmetry that keeps threads failing together.

options.text: If a thread keeps holding A while it spins on B, two threads can spin forever
options.why: Each holds one lock and retries for the other: the circular wait remains, just busy.

options.text: Try-lock with back-off guarantees that every thread eventually succeeds
options.why: Back-off makes success likely, but an unlucky thread can still lose indefinitely.

options.text: Back-off prevents starvation, because waiters are served in arrival order
options.why: Back-off has no queue at all, so it gives no ordering guarantee.

explanation: Try-lock helps only if a thread that fails to get B releases A before retrying; otherwise the circular wait is still there, just with spinning instead of blocking. Releasing and retrying removes deadlock but introduces the risk of livelock, which randomised (often exponential) back-off makes improbable but not impossible. Neither technique guarantees fairness.

stem: A service protects a hot cache with one mutex. Under load, the thread holding it is often descheduled mid-critical-section, and dozens of threads pile up behind it; throughput collapses even though every thread eventually gets the lock. What is this called?

options.text: Deadlock, because the queued threads are all blocked on one lock
options.why: Every thread eventually gets the lock, so nothing is permanently stuck.

options.text: Livelock, because the threads keep retrying without doing work
options.why: The threads are blocked in a queue, not busily retrying.

options.text: A lock convoy: a queue keeps re-forming behind the slow lock holder
options.why: Throughput collapses while the queue drains one waiter at a time.

options.text: Priority inversion, because the queued threads have higher priority
options.why: All threads have equal priority here; the issue is queuing, not priorities.

explanation: A lock convoy forms when a contended lock is held long enough (or its holder is preempted) that many threads queue behind it. Each hand-off involves a context switch, so the convoy keeps re-forming and the lock becomes a serial bottleneck. Remedies include shorter critical sections, lock striping, read-mostly structures and avoiding I/O while holding the lock.
reference: Blasgen et al., The Convoy Phenomenon (1979)

options.text: `notifyAll()` cannot wake a thread waiting on a different monitor
options.why: Both use the same `inner` monitor; the notifier just never reaches it.

options.text: `ready` is not volatile, so the waiter never sees the update
options.why: Both sides access `ready` while holding `inner`, which provides visibility.

options.text: `inner.wait()` frees only `inner`; the notifier waits on `outer`
options.why: The waiter keeps holding `outer` while it waits, so the notifier cannot enter.

options.text: A thread may not call `wait()` while it holds more than one monitor
options.why: Java allows it; the hazard is exactly that the other monitor stays held.

explanation: This is the nested monitor lockout problem. `Object.wait()` releases only the monitor it is called on. The waiter keeps holding `outer`, and the notifier must acquire `outer` before it can set `ready` and notify, so each waits for the other forever. Fixes: never call `wait()` while holding another lock, or use one lock with condition variables.
reference: Java SE docs: Object.wait; Lea, Concurrent Programming in Java, §3.3

stem: A Java service stops responding, and CPU drops to almost zero. You run `jstack <pid>`. What in the output tells you it is a lock deadlock rather than a slow dependency?

options.text: Several threads are in RUNNABLE state inside socket read methods
options.why: Threads blocked in socket reads point to a slow dependency, not a lock cycle.

options.text: The heap summary shows the old generation is almost completely full
options.why: Heap pressure causes GC pauses, not lock cycles.

options.text: A "Found one Java-level deadlock" section listing locks and owners
options.why: jstack detects monitor and ownable-synchronizer cycles and prints them.

options.text: Many threads are in TIMED_WAITING inside `Thread.sleep` calls
options.why: Sleeping threads are idle by design and are not waiting on each other.

explanation: HotSpot's thread dump includes deadlock detection for intrinsic monitors and `java.util.concurrent` ownable synchronizers such as ReentrantLock. When it finds a cycle it prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with each thread, the lock it waits for and the thread that holds it. Taking two or three dumps a few seconds apart also distinguishes a permanent hang from slow progress.

stem: A Python service on Linux is hung. Which two approaches show where every thread is stuck without killing the process? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run `py-spy dump --pid <pid>` to print each thread's Python stack
options.why: py-spy reads the stacks from outside the process without stopping it.

options.text: Send a signal registered earlier with `faulthandler.register(signal.SIGUSR1)`
options.why: faulthandler then dumps every thread's traceback to stderr and keeps running.

options.text: Attach `pdb` with `python -m pdb -p <pid>` to inspect live threads
options.why: pdb has no `-p` attach option; it debugs programs it starts itself.

options.text: Send SIGKILL and read the traceback Python prints as it exits
options.why: SIGKILL ends the process immediately with no traceback.

options.text: Run `strace -p <pid>` to read the Python-level stack of each thread
options.why: strace shows system calls, not Python frames.

explanation: py-spy reads interpreter memory from outside the process and prints Python stacks for all threads. `faulthandler.register(signum)` installs a handler that dumps every thread's traceback when the signal arrives; it must be set up before the hang, and is not available on Windows. Both leave the process running, so you can take several dumps and compare them.

stem: Two PostgreSQL transactions running at READ COMMITTED update rows 1 and 2, but in opposite orders. They can deadlock, and PostgreSQL resolves it by aborting one of them.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: row locks are taken as rows are updated, so opposite orders can form a cycle that the deadlock detector breaks.

options.text: False
options.why: Isolation level does not prevent row-lock deadlocks; UPDATE takes row locks at every level.

explanation: UPDATE acquires row-level locks regardless of isolation level. If transaction 1 locks row 1 and transaction 2 locks row 2, each then waits for the other's row. After `deadlock_timeout` PostgreSQL detects the cycle and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40P01. The documented prevention is to lock rows in a consistent order in every transaction.

stem: A `ThreadPoolExecutor` has 4 workers. Each request task submits one subtask to the same pool and blocks on its result. At most how many request tasks can run concurrently without any risk of starvation deadlock? Type a number.
explanation: If 4 request tasks occupy all 4 workers, their subtasks wait in the queue with no free thread to run on, and all four block forever. With at most 3 request tasks in flight, at least one worker stays free to run queued subtasks one after another, so every request eventually completes. In general, a pool of N needs fewer than N tasks that block on same-pool work, or a separate pool for subtasks.

stem: Thread 1 runs `transfer(a, b)` and thread 2 runs `transfer(b, a)`, each locking the source first and then the destination. Put the events of the interleaving that ends in deadlock in order.

options.text: Thread 1 acquires a.lock
Thread 2 acquires b.lock
Thread 1 requests b.lock and blocks
Thread 2 requests a.lock and blocks, closing the cycle

explanation: Both threads must take their first lock before either takes its second. After that, each holds exactly what the other needs and neither can proceed. If either thread had taken both locks before the other started, there would be no deadlock, which is why such bugs appear intermittently under load.

stem: Service A takes distributed lock X in Redis and then calls service B, which takes distributed lock Y. Another request path takes Y first, then calls A, which needs X. Neither lock has a timeout. Requests hang forever, and no deadlock is ever reported. Why, and what helps?

options.text: Redis detects the cycle but only logs it; enable its deadlock-abort option
options.why: Redis keeps no wait-for graph, so it cannot detect a cycle at all.

options.text: The HTTP calls queue the requests, so this is a convoy, not a deadlock
options.why: Each path holds a lock while waiting for the other's lock: a true cycle.

options.text: Distributed locks cannot deadlock because each lock lives on one server
options.why: Locks on one server can still be acquired in opposite orders by two paths.

options.text: No single component sees the cycle; use lock leases and a global order
options.why: Leases bound how long a lock can be held, and ordering removes the cycle.

explanation: Each local system sees only part of the wait: Redis sees held keys, each service sees a slow call. Nobody builds the global wait-for graph, so the deadlock is silent. Practical defences are lock leases with expiry (plus fencing tokens so a stale holder cannot corrupt data), request timeouts, and a single agreed order for acquiring distributed locks.

stem:
Inside a running asyncio event loop, a coroutine does this. What happens?

```python
async def handler():
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    fut = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(fetch(), loop)
    return fut.result()
```

options.text: It returns `fetch()`'s result once the loop schedules the coroutine
options.why: The loop cannot schedule anything while its thread is blocked in `result()`.

options.text: The loop thread blocks in `result()`, so `fetch()` can never run at all
options.why: `run_coroutine_threadsafe` is for other threads; here the waiter is the loop itself.

options.text: asyncio raises RuntimeError because the coroutine is on the same loop
options.why: Python does not check for this case; the call simply blocks.

options.text: It returns a pending future, because `result()` never blocks in asyncio
options.why: `concurrent.futures.Future.result()` blocks the calling thread.

explanation: `run_coroutine_threadsafe` schedules `fetch()` on `loop` and returns a `concurrent.futures.Future` meant to be waited on from another thread. Calling `.result()` on the loop's own thread blocks that thread, so the loop can never run `fetch()`. Verified on Python 3.13: with `result(timeout=0.5)` it raises TimeoutError. Inside a coroutine, just `await fetch()`.

stem: Same Banker's state as before: 12 units; P0 holds 5 (max 10), P1 holds 2 (max 4), P2 holds 2 (max 9), so 3 are available. P2 now requests 1 more unit. What should the Banker's algorithm do?

options.text: Grant it, because 1 unit is available and P2 is within its declared maximum
options.why: Availability and the maximum are necessary checks but not sufficient ones.

options.text: Grant it, because the system is in a safe state before the request
options.why: Safety is checked for the state after granting, not before it.

options.text: Deny it for now: granting it leads to an unsafe state
options.why: With 2 left, only P1 can finish; then neither P0 nor P2 can.

options.text: Deny it permanently, because granting it would deadlock immediately
options.why: An unsafe state is not yet a deadlock; P2 just waits until it is safe.

explanation: Pretend to grant: available becomes 2, P2 holds 3 and needs 6. P1 (need 2) can finish and return 2, giving 4. Then P0 needs 5 and P2 needs 6, both more than 4, so no safe sequence exists. The algorithm makes P2 wait and retries the request later. An unsafe state means deadlock is possible, not that it has happened (checked with a short simulation).
reference: Silberschatz et al., Operating System Concepts, §8.6.3

stem:
This script prints `start`, then `done` once `outer`'s result times out, but the Python process never exits. Why?

```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, TimeoutError
pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)
def inner(): return 1
def outer(): return pool.submit(inner).result()
print("start")
try:
    pool.submit(outer).result(timeout=1)
except TimeoutError:
    pass
print("done")
```

options.text: Python waits for the pending `inner` task to be cancelled before exiting
options.why: Pending tasks are not the blocker; the stuck worker thread is.

options.text: At exit, Python joins the pool's workers, and one is stuck there forever
options.why: The worker is still blocked inside `outer`, so the join never returns.

options.text: The TimeoutError leaves the pool's internal lock held by the main thread
options.why: A timed-out `result()` releases everything; nothing is left locked.

options.text: The worker thread is a daemon, and daemon threads block interpreter exit
options.why: Daemon threads would not block exit; these workers are not daemon threads.

explanation: The timeout only stops the main thread waiting. The worker is still running `outer`, which waits for `inner`, which waits for that same worker. Since Python 3.9, executor workers are non-daemon threads and an exit hook joins them, so interpreter shutdown waits forever (verified on Python 3.13: the process had to be killed). A deadlocked pool takes down shutdown as well as the request.

stem: A task running on a `ThreadPoolExecutor` worker calls `pool.shutdown(wait=True)` on its own executor. What happens on Python 3.13?

options.text: The call blocks forever, because shutdown waits for the calling worker to finish
options.why: Python detects this case: joining the current thread raises instead of blocking.

options.text: The executor shuts down cleanly and the task carries on and returns normally
options.why: Shutdown tries to join every worker, including the one making the call.

options.text: It raises `RuntimeError: cannot join current thread` inside that task
options.why: shutdown joins all workers, and one of them is the thread calling it.

options.text: It silently skips the calling thread and joins only the other workers
options.why: There is no special case; the join on the current thread raises.

explanation: `shutdown(wait=True)` calls `join()` on every worker thread. When the caller is itself a worker, that includes joining the current thread, which `threading` rejects with `RuntimeError: cannot join current thread`. The exception surfaces from the task's future (verified on Python 3.13). Shutdown belongs to the code that owns the pool, not to tasks running on it.

stem: Which three statements about deadlock prevention, avoidance and detection are correct? (Choose three.)

options.text: Avoidance such as the Banker's algorithm needs each process's maximum claim up front
options.why: The safety check works from declared maximum needs.

options.text: Detection lets deadlocks happen and recovers by aborting or preempting a participant
options.why: This is what databases do with their wait-for-graph detectors.

options.text: Prevention removes one Coffman condition by design, so no runtime check is needed
options.why: For example, a global lock order makes circular wait structurally impossible.

options.text: An unsafe state in the Banker's algorithm means the system is already deadlocked
options.why: Unsafe means a deadlock is possible from here, not that one exists.

options.text: Detection is free, so production databases run it on every single lock request
options.why: Detection has a cost; PostgreSQL waits deadlock_timeout before checking.

explanation: Prevention constrains how resources are requested so a condition can never hold. Avoidance decides at runtime whether granting a request keeps the system in a safe state, which needs advance knowledge of maximum claims. Detection allows deadlocks and recovers. Unsafe states may or may not lead to deadlock, and detection is deliberately delayed because it is not free.
reference: Silberschatz et al., Operating System Concepts, §8.5–8.7

stem:
This version orders locks by account id. A test then calls `transfer(a, a, 10)` (same account, `threading.Lock`). What happens?

```python
def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    first, second = sorted([src, dst], key=lambda acct: acct.id)
    with first.lock:
        with second.lock:
            src.balance -= amount
            dst.balance += amount
```

options.text: It works, because sorting removes duplicates and only one lock is taken
options.why: `sorted` keeps both copies, so `first` and `second` are the same account.

options.text: It deadlocks on itself, taking the same non-reentrant lock twice
options.why: `first.lock` is held, and `second.lock` is the same `Lock`, so the inner `with` never proceeds.

options.text: It raises RuntimeError because a `Lock` cannot be acquired twice
options.why: A second blocking acquire just waits; `Lock` does not detect its owner.

options.text: It completes, but the balance is updated twice in the same transfer
options.why: The thread never reaches the balance updates at all.

explanation: Lock ordering removes the cross-thread cycle but creates a self-deadlock when both arguments are the same account: the inner `with` tries to acquire a `Lock` the thread already holds, and `Lock` is not reentrant. Verified on Python 3.13 (an `acquire(timeout=0.5)` returns False). Handle `src is dst` explicitly, or use an `RLock`.

options.text: Identity hashes can change during GC; cache them in a final field instead
options.why: Identity hash codes are stable for an object's lifetime once assigned.

options.text: The `else` branch should lock `from` first; swapping it fixes the cycle
options.why: The order already depends only on the hashes, except when they are equal.

options.text: Nested `synchronized` blocks cannot be ordered; use a single global lock
options.why: Ordering works fine; the bug is only in how ties are handled.

options.text: Distinct objects can share a hash; on a tie, take a global tiebreak lock
options.why: With equal hashes, each call takes the `else` branch with opposite argument order.

explanation: If two different accounts collide on `identityHashCode`, `transfer(a, b)` locks b then a, while `transfer(b, a)` locks a then b: opposite orders again. Collisions are rare, so the bug shows up only occasionally. Goetz's fix: when the hashes are equal, acquire a static `tieLock` first so only one tied transfer orders itself at a time. Unique account ids avoid the problem entirely.
reference: Goetz, Java Concurrency in Practice, Listing 10.3

options.text: The upgrade succeeds, because the lock is reentrant for the owning thread
options.why: Reentrancy allows read-to-read and write-to-read, but not read-to-write.

options.text: It throws IllegalMonitorStateException because an upgrade is not supported
options.why: No exception is thrown; the write acquire simply waits.

options.text: It blocks forever: the write lock waits for all readers, including itself
options.why: The thread waits for its own read lock to be released, which never happens.

options.text: The read lock is silently converted into the write lock in place
options.why: ReentrantReadWriteLock has no in-place upgrade operation.

explanation: The Javadoc states that downgrading from write to read is allowed, but upgrading from read to write is not possible. The write lock needs every read hold released, and the thread is holding one, so it deadlocks with itself. With two threads both trying to upgrade, it would deadlock even with a hypothetical upgrade. Release the read lock, take the write lock, then re-check (or use `StampedLock.tryConvertToWriteLock`).

stem: An order service often hits PostgreSQL deadlock errors: one code path updates `inventory` rows for items 7 then 3, another path updates 3 then 7. The team wraps transactions in an immediate retry loop, but errors keep piling up at peak. What is the more robust fix?

options.text: Retry faster, with no delay, so the aborted transaction wins the next race
options.why: Immediate retries recreate the same race and can turn deadlocks into livelock.

options.text: Lock the rows in one consistent order, e.g. `ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` first
options.why: If every path locks rows by ascending id, opposite-order cycles cannot form.

options.text: Switch every transaction to SERIALIZABLE isolation to stop the deadlocks
options.why: Row-lock cycles still happen under SERIALIZABLE, and it adds serialization failures.

options.text: Raise `deadlock_timeout` so PostgreSQL stops aborting the transactions
options.why: That only delays detection; the transactions stay stuck for longer.

explanation: Retries are a safety net, not a fix: the root cause is two paths taking the same row locks in opposite orders. Locking all rows a transaction will touch in a deterministic order (for example `SELECT … WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` before updating) breaks circular wait. Keep a retry with jittered back-off for the rare remaining 40P01 errors.

stem: Which two statements about `java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock` fairness are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: A fair lock grants the lock to the longest-waiting thread, at a cost in throughput
options.why: Fair hand-off avoids barging, but forces more context switches.

options.text: The untimed `tryLock()` can grab the lock even when other threads are waiting
options.why: The Javadoc says untimed tryLock does not honour the fairness setting.

options.text: The no-argument `ReentrantLock()` constructor creates a fair lock by default
options.why: The default is non-fair; fairness must be requested with `new ReentrantLock(true)`.

options.text: A fair lock also prevents deadlock, because threads acquire it in order
options.why: Fairness orders waiters for one lock; it does nothing about cycles across locks.

options.text: Fair locks guarantee fair thread scheduling across the whole JVM
options.why: The Javadoc notes lock fairness does not guarantee fair thread scheduling.

explanation: Fair mode favours the longest waiter and prevents starvation of that lock's waiters, but programs using fair locks usually have lower throughput. The default is non-fair, which allows barging. Even on a fair lock, the untimed `tryLock()` barges if the lock is free; `tryLock(0, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` honours fairness. Fairness is unrelated to deadlock across several locks.

stem: Match each production symptom with the liveness failure it most likely indicates.

options.text: Deadlock
Livelock
Starvation
Priority inversion

prompts.text: Several threads are blocked forever, CPU is near 0%, and a thread dump shows a lock cycle
Threads are at 100% CPU, constantly acquiring and releasing locks, but no request completes
Most requests complete normally, but write requests time out under a heavy read load
A high-priority task misses deadlines while a medium-priority task runs and a low-priority task holds its lock

explanation: Deadlock looks idle: blocked threads, no CPU. Livelock looks busy: CPU is burned retrying, with no progress. Starvation means the system progresses but particular work does not, as with writers behind a reader-preferring lock. Priority inversion is a high-priority task indirectly delayed by lower-priority ones. Telling them apart starts with CPU usage and repeated thread dumps.
reference: Herlihy and Shavit, The Art of Multiprocessor Programming, ch. 1

stem: Which two Go programs crash with "fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!"? (Choose two.)

options.text: `main` sends on an unbuffered channel, and no other goroutine exists
options.why: main is the only goroutine and it is blocked, so the runtime aborts.

options.text: `main` ends with an empty `select {}` and starts no other goroutines
options.why: An empty select blocks forever; with nothing else running, all goroutines are asleep.

options.text: `main` sends once on a channel created with `make(chan int, 1)`
options.why: The buffer has room for one value, so the send completes without blocking.

options.text: A worker goroutine is stuck on a channel while `main` blocks in `http.ListenAndServe`
options.why: main is blocked on network I/O, which the detector does not treat as asleep.

options.text: A leaked goroutine waits forever on a channel while `main` returns normally
options.why: The program exits when main returns; leaked goroutines do not crash it.

explanation: The runtime's check fires only when every goroutine is blocked on channels, select or sync primitives with no way to wake. A goroutine waiting on network I/O or a timer counts as possibly runnable, so partial deadlocks in servers go undetected and need goroutine dumps (SIGQUIT or pprof) to diagnose. A goroutine leak in a program that exits is silent.
reference: Go runtime source: checkdead; Go spec: Select statements

options.text: `available` is not thread-safe; switch to a ConcurrentHashMap-backed set
options.why: The data structure is protected by Dispatcher's lock; that is not the deadlock.

options.text: Each class calls the other while holding its own lock; use open calls
options.why: setLocation goes Taxi→Dispatcher while getImage goes Dispatcher→Taxi.

options.text: Synchronized methods are not reentrant; use ReentrantLock in both classes
options.why: Synchronized is reentrant; the problem is two different locks in opposite orders.

options.text: `getImage` holds the lock too long; add a timeout to each synchronized call
options.why: Synchronized blocks cannot time out, and the cycle is about order, not duration.

explanation: setLocation holds the Taxi lock and calls Dispatcher.notifyAvailable (needs the Dispatcher lock). getImage holds the Dispatcher lock and calls Taxi.getLocation (needs a Taxi lock): opposite order across collaborating objects. The fix is open calls: hold a lock only to read or update local state, then call the other object after releasing it (for example copy the taxi list, then iterate without the lock).

stem: A production service is hung. Put the steps of a sound deadlock diagnosis in order.

options.text: Capture thread dumps of the live process several seconds apart
Compare the dumps to find threads blocked in the same frames every time
Find the cycle and the code paths that acquire those locks in opposite orders
Map which thread holds and which waits for each lock, building a wait-for graph
Fix the acquisition order or narrow the critical sections, then add a regression test

explanation: Several dumps distinguish permanently blocked threads from slow ones. Owner and waiter information (jstack prints it; Go goroutine dumps and py-spy show the blocked frames) gives the wait-for graph, and the cycle points to the code paths. Fixing the order is the real remedy; a stress test that drives both paths concurrently guards against regressions.
reference: Oracle docs: Troubleshooting Guide, Hung Processes

stem: In PostgreSQL, which statement about deadlock handling is correct?

options.text: The youngest transaction in the cycle is always the one that gets aborted
options.why: PostgreSQL makes no such promise; the victim is not predictable.

options.text: Deadlocks are checked the instant any lock wait starts
options.why: The check runs only after a wait has lasted `deadlock_timeout`.

options.text: Deadlocks cannot occur at READ COMMITTED, only at SERIALIZABLE
options.why: Row-lock deadlocks occur at every isolation level.

options.text: One transaction is aborted, and which one is hard to predict
options.why: The docs say not to rely on which one; applications must handle and retry.

explanation: PostgreSQL automatically detects deadlocks and resolves them by aborting one of the transactions involved; the docs say exactly which one is difficult to predict and should not be relied upon. Detection runs after a lock wait exceeds `deadlock_timeout` (default 1s), which keeps the check cheap for short waits. Applications should retry 40P01 errors and, better, lock in a consistent order.
